data.title: <![CDATA[White House Withdraws Dr. Heidi Overton’s Nomination as FDA Commissioner: Report]]>
data.description:
The White House has pulled its of Dr. Heidi Overton as FDA commissioner amid skepticism from multiple Senate Republicans, according to a White House official and two other people familiar with the matter.

The decision comes the night before a Senate committee was due to vote on whether to advance her nomination.

A vote that never happened

Sen. Bill Cassidy, the committee’s chair, maintained Tuesday night that Dr. Overton was on the verge of garnering enough support. In a post on X shortly after her nomination was pulled, Cassidy wrote: “Tonight, the White House abandoned a viable confirmation path for Dr. Overton.” He says the withdrawal was odd given that he had been having productive conversations with members, and that he believed she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate. “I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate. My conversations with her convinced me she would follow the science and push back against decisions that put Americans’ health at risk,” wrote Cassidy.

data.title: <![CDATA[Pfizer, Verismo Strike Licensing Deals to Push CAR T Manufacturing In Vivo]]>
data.description:
A pair of licensing agreements this week pushed CAR T cell therapy into new territory, with two companies moving to engineer T cells directly inside the body rather than relying on today’s weeks-long manufacturing process.

Verismo Therapeutics licenses in vivo CAR T technology

Verismo Therapeutics entered an agreement to license the Pack-it technology enabling in vivo engineering of KIR-CAR T cells from Stanford Medicine. The agreement provides Verismo with technology from the lab of Crystal Mackall, MD, Ernest and Amelia Gallo Family professor, professor of pediatrics and medicine at Stanford Medicine, and founding director of the Stanford Center for Cancer Cell Therapy.1

The deal will allow Verismo to extend its multi-chain KIR-CAR platform into next-generation in vivo delivery of KIR-CAR T cell therapies, with the potential to reduce time-to-treatment and cost and broaden patient access over time.1 Verismo’s platform is designed to take CAR T therapy beyond the single-chain limitations of current approaches, with the potential to deliver durable anti-tumor responses while minimizing off-target toxicity. The platform is currently advancing in two Phase I clinical trials: Synkir-110 in solid tumors and Synkir-310 in B-cell malignancies.1 Both trials have generated early positive signals presented at the American Association for Cancer Research 2026 Annual Meeting.

data.title: <![CDATA[Gilead Signs Royalty-Free Licensing Deals to Broaden Access to Obeldesivir ]]>
data.description:
Gilead Sciences signed royalty-free voluntary licensing agreements with three generic manufacturers to support potential future access to its investigational antiviral obeldesivir as post-exposure prophylaxis for Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease.

The agreements will cover 127 primarily low- and lower-middle-income countries, including all African countries that have reported cases during the current Ebola BVD outbreak.1 The move signals Gilead’s effort to get ahead of a currently ongoing outbreak by lining up manufacturing and supply capacity before clinical results are even in.

The geographic scope of the new agreements mirrors Gilead’s existing voluntary licensing arrangements for remdesivir in Covid-19, with the agreements being designed to support manufacturing readiness, technology transfer, and supply planning, while a field trial evaluating obeldesivir continues.1

What do the agreements cover?

The royalty-free licenses allow Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories, Eva Pharma, and Ferozsons Laboratories to manufacture and supply obeldesivir in the licensed territory, contingent on clinical data and applicable regulatory authorizations.1 Technology transfer discussions are already underway with these three manufacturers, with Gilead saying agreements with additional manufacturers are under discussion.

data.title: <![CDATA[FDA Approves Cosentyx for Polymyalgia Rheumatica, Wilserdly for ER-Positive ESR1-Mutated Advanced Breast Cancer ]]>
data.description:
Two new treatments in rheumatology and oncology secured key FDA approvals this week, each addressing diseases where treatment options have remained limited for years.

Novartis wins FDA approval for Cosentyx

FDA approved Cosentyx (secukinumab) 150 mg for adult patients with polymyalgia rheumatica who have had an inadequate response to corticosteroids or who cannot tolerate corticosteroid taper.

The approval makes Cosentyx the first and only anti-interleukin-17 biologic cleared for people living with polymyalgia rheumatica, a common inflammatory disease that primarily affects adults over 50, giving physicians a new option beyond the long-term steroid use that has long served as the standard of care.1

data.title: <![CDATA[M&A Roundup: Johnson & Johnson Acquires Ollin Biosciences, Eli Lilly Acquires Calytrix Bio, AmyriAD Therpaeutics Acquires AD04 Alzheimers Program, Sanofi Enters Collaboration with Seawolf Therapeutics ]]>
data.description:
A wave of new transactions this week is funneling capital and deal-making activity into some of biopharma’s most closely watched disease areas, from retinal disease and blood cancers to Alzheimer’s and next-generation gene delivery.

Johnson & Johnson acquires Ollin Biosciences

Johnson & Johnson has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Ollin Biosciences, Inc. for $2.2 billion upfront, with the potential for additional regulatory and commercial milestone payments of up to approximately $1.125 billion.1 Johnson & Johnson is also set to enter into a separate development funding agreement with Blackstone Life Sciences, under which Blackstone will pay a total of $750 million to Johnson & Johnson over multiple years to fully fund the Phase III development of OLN324, contingent upon the acquisition’s close.

In return, Blackstone will be eligible to receive certain regulatory and sales milestone payments, as well as single-digit royalties. The transaction is expected to close before the end of 2026, subject to applicable regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions.

Eli Lilly agrees to acquire Calytrix Bio

Calytrix Bio, Inc. announced a definitive agreement for Eli Lilly and Company to acquire the company, with Calytrix shareholders eligible to receive up to $1.5 billion in cash, inclusive of an upfront payment and subsequent payments tied to the achievement of certain clinical and regulatory milestones.2
